title: How to Host Your Website for Free with GitHub
summary: Explains web hosting (moving a site's files from your own machine onto an always-online web server) and then walks through publishing the HTML Portfolio project for free with GitHub Pages: create a public repository, upload the folder's contents, and switch Pages on for the main branch.

concepts.heading: Local development vs web hosting
points: Local development: every HTML file, image and folder sits on your own computer, so only you can open the site.
Sharing a local site would mean handing over a copy of the files (like the course's zipped downloads), which is not a real website.
A web server is a computer permanently connected to the internet that serves the files it holds to anyone who requests them.
Web hosting = putting your site's files (index.html, other pages, images) onto such a server so the site gets a public address.

concepts.heading: Why index.html matters
points: GitHub Pages serves the file named index.html at the top level of the repository as the home page.
The name must be exactly index.html, all lowercase. home.html, me.html or Index.html will not become the landing page.
Upload your finished index.html, not the starter version that only had TODO comments.
(Extra) Most web servers follow the same convention: a folder URL returns that folder's index.html.

concepts.heading: GitHub repository settings used
points: Repository name: html-portfolio (it becomes part of the live URL). Description is optional.
Visibility must be Public so anyone can view the hosted site.
Tick 'Add a README file' at creation. The repo then opens on the normal file view with Add file > Upload files available.
Clicking Commit changes after uploading records the files on the main branch at the root (/), which is what Pages publishes. Git itself is covered properly in a later section.
(Extra) The live address follows the pattern https://<username>.github.io/html-portfolio/. Free Pages hosting needs a public repo.

concepts.heading: Relative paths make hosting just work
points: (Extra) The portfolio's relative links (./public/..., ./assets/images/...) work identically locally and on github.io as long as the folder structure is uploaded unchanged; an absolute path to your own disk would break once hosted.
(Extra) The Pages server is case-sensitive: Images/Preview.png will not find images/preview.png, even if it worked on your Mac or PC.

task.name: Put the HTML Portfolio online with GitHub Pages
task.starting_point: The completed HTML Portfolio project from the previous lesson on your computer: index.html with your code, a public folder with the other pages, and assets/images with the preview screenshots.
task.goal: A live, shareable URL that shows the portfolio exactly as it looks locally, with every link and image working.
steps: Go to github.com and sign up for a free account, or sign in if you already have one.
Use the + menu in the top-right corner and choose New repository.
Name it html-portfolio, optionally add a description, set visibility to Public, and tick Add a README file. Click Create repository.
On the new repo page, open the Add file dropdown and choose Upload files.

In your file manager, open the portfolio project folder. Confirm index.html is spelled exactly that, lowercase, and contains your finished code; confirm the images folder holds the previews and public holds the other pages.
Select the contents of the project folder (index.html, public, assets) and drag them into the upload area. Do not drag the outer folder itself.
Click Commit changes. Processing can take a few minutes; refresh until every file and folder appears in the repo listing. Re-upload anything missing.
Open the repo's Settings tab, then Pages in the sidebar.
Under Build and deployment > Branch, change None to main (root folder /) and click Save.
Refresh the Pages screen until a banner says the site is live at a github.io address. This can take roughly 1 to 10 minutes; if you see an error such as no server being available, wait and try again.
Click Visit site, click through every page and image to check it matches the local version, then share the URL (the course suggests posting it in the Q&A).
task.expected_result: A public github.io URL serving the portfolio home page, with working links to the project pages, About Me and Contact Me, and visible preview images.
task.reference_repo_path: Section 04 - Multi-Page Websites/04.03 - HTML Portfolio Project

pitfalls: Dragging the whole project folder into the upload box. The repo root then has no index.html, so the Pages URL shows a 404 or the README instead of the portfolio.
Home page renamed (home.html, me.html) or capitalised (Index.html).
Skipping the README checkbox, which leaves the empty-repo setup screen instead of the upload option.
Expecting the site instantly. Deployment can take several minutes, and transient server errors usually clear on retry.

playground.coverage: No dedicated hosting lesson. The portfolio lesson's notes only say the page will eventually go online with GitHub Pages; nothing explains web servers, local vs hosted, or the Pages workflow.
gaps_and_ideas: Add a short 4.4 'Publish it' lesson (or a section at the end of s04-portfolio): blurb 'Hosting means copying your files onto a computer that never switches off and is always online.' with a local-vs-server diagram.

Tasks: (1) check the root file is named index.html; (2) list the folder contents you will upload and spot the wrong one (the parent folder); (3) predict the live URL for public/about.html given a username; (4) find and fix a link that only works locally (absolute C:\ path) and one that breaks on a case-sensitive server.
